content: Mobile health, commonly referred to as mHealth, is a subset of eHealth. Although there is no universally accepted definition, the Global Observatory for eHealth (GOe) defines mHealth as the practice of medicine and public health supported by mobile devices. These devices include mobile phones, patient monitoring devices, personal digital assistants (PDAs), and other wireless technologies. mHealth leverages the basic functionalities of mobile phones, such as voice calls and short messaging services (SMS), as well as more advanced features like general packet radio service (GPRS), 3G and 4G telecommunications systems, global positioning systems (GPS), and Bluetooth technology. Given the increasing integration of technology into daily life, it is reasonable to anticipate that mHealth will become a fundamental component of healthcare delivery. An observational study revealed that most patients own a smartphone and are interested in using it to enhance their health, even among populations with lower socioeconomic status where access might be a concern. However, certain limitations exist, such as the accuracy of smartphone accelerometers in estimating energy expenditure. Additionally, the usability and functionality of mobile health applications have been questioned. Incorporating gamification into these applications may enhance their effectiveness. Effectiveness of mHealth Patient Compliance Mobile phone-based strategies for improving medication adherence have shown mixed results. For primary prevention of cardiovascular disease, mobile phone interventions have demonstrated low-quality evidence in improving medication compliance. However, a meta-analysis of 16 randomized controlled trials involving patients with chronic diseases found that text messaging nearly doubled the odds of medication adherence. This intervention increased adherence rates from 50% to 67.8%, representing an absolute improvement of 17.8%. More recent trials have confirmed these benefits. In the context of physical activity, a 2018 proof-of-concept randomized controlled trial demonstrated that fitness trackers could promote behavioral changes, such as goal setting and social support, within the framework of social cognitive therapy. These trackers, combined with counseling using motivational interviewing, were found to enhance physical activity. These findings align with a prior systematic review conducted on overweight individuals. Patient Engagement mHealth has the potential to enhance patient engagement. A prospective randomized controlled trial found that participants using a mobile application to monitor their chronic disease exhibited improved health self-management compared to those who did not use such an application. Patient Outcomes Currently, there is limited evidence to suggest that mobile phone messaging interventions directly improve health outcomes. However, these interventions may enhance a patient’s ability to self-manage their condition. However, the study focusing on asthma reported a significant improvement in pooled asthma symptom scores favoring the text messaging intervention. All four studies demonstrated improved disease self-monitoring or medication adherence with mobile phone messaging. For coronary artery disease, a randomized controlled trial showed a reduction in risk factors associated with mHealth use. In contrast, a trial on hypertension found no benefit. Meta-analyses published in 2019, including a review of randomized trials through May 2017 and an AHRQ technical brief of studies through July 2017, indicated that mHealth interventions augmented by healthcare providers or study personnel were beneficial. A trial excluded from these reviews demonstrated a greater reduction in hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), and a more recent trial also reported a decline in HbA1c levels. Physical Activity Systematic reviews conducted in 2020 and 2016 concluded that mHealth interventions increase physical activity. Text messaging has been shown to provide short-term improvements. Trials and reviews suggest that performance feedback from mobile devices regarding progress toward goals can enhance motivation. Weight Loss and Obesity A systematic review conducted for the Community Guide found that electronic activity monitors effectively increase physical activity. However, a 2014 randomized controlled trial involving 212 patients with a body mass index (BMI) greater than 25 kg/m² evaluated the efficacy of the MyFitnessPal application for weight loss in a primary care setting. The study found no significant difference in weight loss between the application group and usual care. Notably, most participants stopped using the application after the first month, with 94 participants logging in during the first month compared to only 34 by the sixth month. A second randomized controlled trial also yielded negative results. A 2013 pilot randomized controlled trial found that a smartphone application might improve adherence and total weight loss after six months compared to a website monitoring group. In this study, 128 overweight individuals were randomized to receive a weight management intervention via a smartphone app, a website, or a paper diary. The smartphone app, My Meal Mate (MMM), was developed using an evidence-based behavioral approach. Trial retention rates were 93% in the smartphone group, 55% in the website group, and 53% in the paper diary group at six months. Adherence rates were highest in the smartphone group, with a mean of 92 days, compared to 35 days in the website group and 29 days in the paper diary group. Mean weight loss and BMI reduction at six months were -4.6 kg and -1.6 kg/m² in the smartphone group, -2.9 kg and -1.0 kg/m² in the paper diary group, and -1.3 kg and -0.5 kg/m² in the website group. Diagnostic Assistance Preliminary research suggests that smartphone cameras may be capable of detecting atrial fibrillation using photoplethysmography.
